subject: Mass Media / Mass Communication (Code: 318)
past_paper_reference: CUET UG Mass Media Past Papers (2022-2024)

questions.question: In information theory and communication models, any extraneous physical factor (such as loud static, passing traffic, or poor microphone connections) that interferes with the transmission of a message is called:
options: A) Physical (or Channel) Noise
B) Psychological Noise
C) Semantic Distortion
D) Cultural Dissonance
questions.explanation: Physical noise refers to environmental or technical interference in the communication channel that impairs signal transmission.

questions.question: In non-verbal communication, personal objects such as clothing, jewelry, hairstyles, tattoos, and eyeglasses that communicate an individual's identity, status, and lifestyle are termed:
options: A) Proxemics
B) Artifacts (or Objectics)
C) Chronemics
D) Haptics
questions.explanation: Artifacts (or object language) include clothing, accessories, cars, and adornments that non-verbally project personality, socioeconomic status, and cultural affiliation.

questions.question: Frank Dance's 1967 'Helical Spiral Model' of communication is conceptually innovative because it depicts communication not as a closed circle, but as an ever-expanding helix that:
options: A) Stops abruptly whenever the speaker takes a physical breath
B) Reverses backwards into total silence after sixty seconds of speech
C) Evolves continuously forward through time, where past communicative experiences cumulatively influence and expand future interactions
D) Operates identically to a static mathematical equation without any changes
questions.explanation: Dance's helical spiral represents communication as a dynamic, continuous, non-linear evolutionary process where each interaction expands upon cumulative prior experience.

questions.question: According to Robert Entman's seminal formulation of 'Framing' in news journalism, to frame an issue means to:
options: A) Construct wooden picture frames around physical front-page newspaper articles
B) Falsely frame innocent criminal suspects by forging police fingerprint records
C) Photograph news events through a decorative round brass telescope lens
D) Select certain aspects of a perceived reality and make them more salient in a communicating text, thereby defining problems, diagnosing causes, making moral judgments, and suggesting remedies
questions.explanation: Entman showed framing selects and highlights specific facets of an issue to promote a particular problem definition, causal interpretation, moral evaluation, and treatment recommendation.

questions.question: In media psychology and political communication, how does the 'Priming Effect' operate in relation to public evaluation of political leaders?
options: A) By giving heavy coverage to certain issues (e.g., national defense or inflation), the media primes citizens to use those specific standards when judging a political leader's overall performance
B) The media paints a layer of chemical white primer over television broadcast studio walls
C) The media forces political candidates to deliver speeches in rhyming poetic couplets
D) The media replaces all television debate moderators with robotic computers
questions.explanation: Priming is an extension of agenda-setting: by making certain issues accessible in audience memory, media shapes the benchmarks citizens use to evaluate politicians.

questions.sub_topic: Walter Benjamin: The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction (1936)
questions.question: In his historic 1936 essay 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction', cultural theorist Walter Benjamin argued that mass technological reproduction (photography, cinema) fundamentally destroys an artwork's:
options: A) Commercial financial market price in international stock exchanges
B) 'Aura'—its unique, authentic presence in physical time and space tied to ritual and tradition
C) Chemical pigment composition when exposed to ultraviolet daylight
D) Ability to be viewed by working-class industrial factory laborers
questions.explanation: Benjamin argued that mechanical reproduction strips art of its 'aura' (its singular presence, authenticity, and cult value), democratizing art while transforming it into a political instrument.

questions.sub_topic: Umberto Eco: Aberrant Decoding in Mass Media (1965)
questions.question: Italian semiotician Umberto Eco introduced the concept of 'Aberrant Decoding' to explain what phenomenon in mass media communication?
options: A) When computer television decoders suffer physical electrical hardware failures during storms
B) When journalists publish news reports using secret encrypted wartime military ciphers
C) When audiences decode a mass media message using a cultural code different from the sender's code, producing an interpretation radically divergent from what the sender intended
D) When radio listeners fall asleep while listening to classical symphony orchestra broadcasts
questions.explanation: Eco demonstrated that mass media frequently produces aberrant decoding because mass senders and heterogeneous, culturally diverse receivers do not share identical semiotic codes.

questions.question: In a printed or digital newspaper article, the line appearing at the beginning or end of the story that credits the individual reporter who authored the article is the:
options: A) Headline
B) Dateline
C) Masthead
D) Byline
questions.explanation: A byline credits the journalist who reported and wrote the story, establishing individual accountability and authorship.

questions.question: When an interviewee agrees to speak to an investigative reporter strictly 'Off the Record', what is the binding ethical professional agreement?
options: A) The information is provided purely for the reporter's background understanding and cannot be published, quoted, or attributed to the source under any form
B) The reporter must record the interview on vinyl phonograph record discs
C) The information can be published immediately with the source's full name and photograph
D) The interview must be conducted while both parties stand outdoors on a sports running track
questions.explanation: 'Off the record' information cannot be published or attributed in any form; it serves solely to guide the reporter's understanding and point toward independent, verifiable leads.

questions.question: Unlike a signed news report or feature article, what makes the official 'Editorial' (Leader) of a newspaper unique in journalistic voice?
options: A) It is written exclusively by junior high school student interns during summer vacations
B) It represents the institutional voice and collective philosophical stance of the newspaper as an institution on major public issues, traditionally appearing unsigned
C) It contains only commercial retail coupons for household kitchen appliances
D) It is printed in invisible ink that becomes readable only under specialized studio lamps
questions.explanation: The editorial expresses the institutional opinion, stance, and philosophy of the publication as a collective entity, typically published anonymously on the editorial page.

questions.sub_topic: Conflict and Human Interest as News Values
questions.question: Why do international news organizations prioritize stories involving political rivalries, labor strikes, and courtroom litigation over routine bureaucratic agreements?
options: A) Because reporters are legally barred from writing about peaceful community gatherings
B) Because conflict stories cost zero money to investigate compared to peaceful stories
C) Because 'Conflict' is a foundational news value that naturally generates dramatic tension, emotional resonance, and reveals competing societal interests
D) Because printing presses can only print dramatic words when machines operate at top speed
questions.explanation: Conflict is a core news value: clashing perspectives, controversies, and struggles inherently create narrative stakes, public drama, and highlight systemic friction.

questions.sub_topic: Data Journalism Workflow: Cleaning, Scraping, Visualizing
questions.question: In contemporary data journalism, what sequence of technical steps constitutes the core empirical investigation workflow?
options: A) Headline Writing -> Printing -> Delivery -> Shredding
B) Interviewing -> Audio Recording -> Radio Broadcast -> Cassette Sale
C) Photography -> Darkroom Developing -> Framing -> Gallery Exhibition
D) Data Gathering (Scraping/FOIA) -> Data Cleaning (Normalization) -> Data Analysis (Verification) -> Data Visualization (Storytelling)
questions.explanation: Data journalism follows a scientific pipeline: gathering raw data (scraping/APIs), cleaning and verifying anomalies, interrogating with statistical tools, and visualizing narrative insights.

questions.sub_topic: Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (1973): Newsprint Policy
questions.question: In the landmark constitutional case 'Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India' (1973), the Supreme Court struck down the Government's Newsprint Control Policy because:
options: A) Limiting newsprint quotas and capping newspaper page numbers to ten pages directly restricted press circulation and editorial content, violating Article 19(1)(a)
B) Newsprint paper was found to be chemically contaminated with industrial pollutants
C) The Times of India had failed to register its trademark under the Trade Marks Act
D) Newspapers were legally classified as electronic broadcasting transmitters under the Telegraph Act
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court ruled that regulating newsprint to cap newspaper pages and circulation directly curbed freedom of speech, declaring: 'The press has the right of free propagation and circulation of ideas.'

questions.question: Why is 'Checkbook Journalism'—the practice of paying financial fees to sources or eyewitnesses in exchange for exclusive interviews—universally condemned in professional ethics codes?
options: A) Because banks charge high processing transaction fees on corporate check payments
B) It incentivizes sources to sensationalize, exaggerate, or invent dramatic falsehoods to maximize their financial payout, severely compromising the veracity of public information
C) Because journalists are prohibited by law from carrying bank checkbooks into newsroom offices
D) Because sources are legally required to surrender seventy percent of all interview money to the police
questions.explanation: Paying for interviews corrupts journalistic integrity: financial incentives encourage witnesses to tailor, embellish, or fabricate testimony to fetch higher fees, distorting truth.

questions.question: When a multinational sports brand hires a famous world-champion cricketer to wear its athletic footwear in television advertisements, it uses the strategy of:
options: A) Subliminal Hypnosis
B) Astroturfing
C) Celebrity Endorsement
D) Negative Political Bashing
questions.explanation: Celebrity endorsement leverages the fame, trust, and aspirational appeal of well-known figures to enhance brand credibility, recall, and purchase intent.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Public Relations
questions.question: What is the primary role of a specialized external Public Relations (PR) consultancy agency hired by a commercial corporation?
options: A) To physically manufacture automobile engines in industrial factory assembly lines
B) To write supreme judicial rulings for civil district court trials
C) To audit the physical plumbing systems of municipal government hospitals
D) To build, manage, and protect the corporation's public reputation, coordinate media relations, and navigate crisis communications
questions.explanation: PR agencies specialize in strategic communication, reputation management, media relations, stakeholder engagement, and crisis mitigation for client organizations.

questions.question: In advertising copy design, how does an 'Emotional Appeal' differ from a 'Rational Appeal'?
options: A) An emotional appeal connects with consumer feelings, love, humor, pride, or fear, whereas a rational appeal emphasizes objective product features, price, efficiency, and verifiable performance facts
B) An emotional appeal uses only black-and-white print text, while a rational appeal uses color video
C) An emotional appeal can only be broadcast during midnight hours, while a rational appeal airs in daytime
D) An emotional appeal is legally prohibited from mentioning the registered brand name
questions.explanation: Rational appeals target the logical intellect with factual features, specs, and price/quality data; emotional appeals tap psychological desires, warmth, status, humor, or safety.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Public Relations
questions.question: In corporate communication theory, what is the distinction between 'Corporate Identity' and 'Corporate Image'?
options: A) Corporate identity refers to the physical architecture of the corporate headquarters building

B) Corporate Identity is how the organization defines itself and projects its values (logos, design, behavior), whereas Corporate Image is the external perception of that organization held by the public
C) Corporate image is the monetary tax paid by the corporation to municipal authorities
D) There is zero difference; both terms refer to the corporation's legal incorporation certificate
questions.explanation: Corporate Identity is sender-oriented (what the company projects via philosophy, design, ethos); Corporate Image is receiver-oriented (how the public perceives the company).

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Advertising Media
questions.question: Commercial advertisements placed on public transport vehicles—such as wraps on city buses, metro train interiors, taxi roofs, and auto-rickshaw backs—are classified as:
options: A) Direct Response Telemarketing
B) Search Engine Sponsored Links
C) Transit Advertising (part of Out-of-Home)
D) Interactive Streaming Podcasts
questions.explanation: Transit advertising is a mobile sub-segment of Out-of-Home (OOH) advertising displayed on public transport vehicles, targeting urban commuters on the move.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Advertising Ethics
questions.question: In contemporary advertising ethics and consumer protection, the deceptive corporate practice of 'Greenwashing' involves:
options: A) Painting the corporate office walls with green non-toxic organic paint
B) Planting ten thousand fruit trees in rural agricultural community villages
C) Manufacturing digital computer processors out of recycled aluminum cans
D) Disseminating misleading or exaggerated environmental claims to market products as eco-friendly and sustainable when the company's actual operations remain ecologically destructive
questions.explanation: Greenwashing deceives environmentally conscious consumers by using eco-friendly imagery, buzzwords ('organic', 'carbon-neutral'), and PR spin to mask ongoing unsustainable practices.

questions.question: Which basic television camera shot frames a human subject tightly from the top of the head down to the shoulders, emphasizing subtle facial expressions and emotional intensity?
options: A) Close-Up (CU)
B) Extreme Long Shot (ELS)
C) Aerial Drone Shot
D) Worm's Eye View
questions.explanation: A Close-Up (CU) isolates the head and neck, drawing viewer focus directly to the subject's facial expressions, emotional nuances, and eyes.

questions.question: In the standard three-point television lighting triangle, which light source is the principal, brightest illuminator of the subject, establishing the scene's primary angle of illumination?
options: A) Fill Light
B) Key Light
C) Back Light
D) Kicker Light
questions.explanation: The Key Light is the dominant, primary light source in three-point lighting, illuminating the subject and setting the scene's overall exposure, mood, and shadow structure.

questions.question: In television and film camerawork, why must a director strictly maintain the '180-Degree Rule' (Axis of Action) during dialogue scenes between two actors?
options: A) To prevent the television studio camera batteries from overheating in warm weather
B) To ensure that actors turn their backs to the camera for exactly half of the program
C) To maintain consistent left-to-right spatial screen direction, preventing disorienting jumps where characters appear to switch physical positions on screen
D) To reduce the physical electrical wattage consumed by overhead studio lighting grids
questions.explanation: The 180-degree rule draws an imaginary axis between two characters; keeping cameras on one side of this line preserves consistent screen direction and spatial orientation.

questions.question: In television broadcast news, what is the primary operational domain of the 'Executive Producer' (or Show Producer)?
options: A) Operating the video switcher console keys to cut between camera inputs
B) Physically holding the overhead boom microphone pole on the studio floor
C) Applying theatrical stage makeup and hair spray to news anchors
D) Overall creative and editorial supervision of the broadcast, managing rundown timing, approving story lineups, coordinating budgets, and guiding the director
questions.explanation: The Producer manages the overarching production: conceptualizing the show rundown, deciding content lineup, balancing timings, managing staff, and overseeing editorial quality.

questions.sub_topic: Cutaway Shot Function in News Editing
questions.question: In television news editing, what is the practical purpose of inserting a 'Cutaway' shot (such as a reporter nodding or a close-up of an interviewee's hands)?
options: A) To break up continuous footage of an interview, bridge edits, and conceal jump cuts caused by trimming repetitive or redundant spoken dialogue
B) To show the audience a live satellite map of the national electrical grid system
C) To allow the television news anchor to exit the studio and drink water for ten minutes
D) To permanently delete the audio soundtrack recorded by the field camera crew
questions.explanation: Cutaways cut away from the primary subject to related action or reaction shots (cut-in/cutaway), smoothly masking edits in interview footage and preventing jump cuts.

questions.question: How did the introduction of Direct-To-Home (DTH) satellite television in India (such as DD Free Dish and private DTH providers) fundamentally alter broadcast distribution geography?
options: A) It required every Indian household to lay physical underground copper cables to regional post offices

B) It bypassed local terrestrial cable operators by beaming digital television signals directly from geostationary communication satellites to small consumer dish antennas, reaching remote rural regions
C) It banned all private commercial television channels, allowing only state agricultural bulletins
D) It forced televisions to operate on direct solar energy without using electrical wall plugs
questions.explanation: DTH bypassed local cable operators (LCOs) and terrestrial transmitters, using Ku-band satellite transponders to beam digital broadcasts directly to rooftop dishes nationwide.

questions.question: In radio and television studio operations, a pre-arranged signal (such as a red studio tally light or a floor manager's pointed finger) that instructs an on-air presenter to start speaking is a:
options: A) Slate
B) Slug
C) Cue
D) Scoop
questions.explanation: A cue is a verbal or visual signal directing talent or technicians to begin speaking, execute an action, roll music, or initiate a transition.

questions.question: In audio physics and sound recording, the volume or loudness of a sound wave is determined by its amplitude and is measured in:
options: A) Hertz (Hz)
B) Kelvin (K)
C) Megapixels (MP)
D) Decibels (dB)
questions.explanation: Amplitude corresponds to sound pressure level and perceived loudness, measured logarithmically in Decibels (dB).

questions.question: In producing an immersive radio drama, how does a sound director establish that a scene is taking place inside a noisy moving train at midnight?
options: A) By layering rhythmic locomotive wheel clicks (track sound effects), a distant mournful whistle, muffled engine rumble, and localized conversational dialogue
B) By verbally shouting the word 'TRAIN' fifty times into the studio microphone
C) By forcing listeners to look at printed train tickets mailed to their home addresses
D) By shutting down the radio transmitter so listeners can imagine silence
questions.explanation: Radio drama creates sensory environments through acoustic codes: layering environmental soundscapes, rhythmic SFX, and localized voices to construct rich mental worlds.

questions.question: Why is a 'Cardioid' (heart-shaped) pickup pattern the most popular microphone choice for radio talk studio hosts?
options: A) It records sound exclusively from the ceiling and rejects sound from the presenter's mouth
B) It picks up sound primarily from the front of the capsule while rejecting sound from the rear, minimizing unwanted room reverberation and adjacent presenter spill
C) It changes human voices into classical musical flute notes automatically
D) It requires the studio engineer to wear specialized heart-shaped eyeglasses
questions.explanation: Cardioid microphones have a heart-shaped directional pickup pattern sensitive to sound from the front and rejecting sound from the rear, minimizing room echo and crosstalk.

questions.sub_topic: All India Radio (AIR) Historical Renaming as Akashvani
questions.question: In Indian broadcasting history, when was the poetic name 'Akashvani' (Voice from the Sky)—coined by scholar M.V. Gopalaswamy for his private Mysore station in 1935—officially adopted for All India Radio?
questions.explanation: All India Radio officially adopted the name 'Akashvani' ('voice from the skies') for its domestic services in 1956, honoring the name coined by Dr. M.V. Gopalaswamy in Mysore in 1935.

questions.question: In professional radio broadcasting and podcast audio mixing, how does automated 'Audio Ducking' function?
options: A) It plays recorded waterfowl bird sounds whenever the presenter makes a factual error on air
B) It permanently deletes all audio tracks whenever computer processor temperatures rise
C) It converts spoken English sentences into automated mechanical Morse code chirps
D) It automatically lowers the volume level of a background music bed whenever the voiceover presenter speaks into the microphone, restoring music volume when they pause
questions.explanation: Audio ducking (sidechain compression) automatically attenuates background music when a voice signal exceeds a threshold, keeping spoken commentary prominent and intelligible.

questions.question: In the collaborative art of motion picture production, who is the principal artistic visionary who oversees actors' performances, guides camera placement, and shapes the overall visual storytelling?
options: A) Film Director
B) Production Accountant
C) Costume Fabric Buyer
D) Theater Ticket Usher
questions.explanation: The Director is the creative head of the film, guiding actors, visual framing, shot pacing, and aesthetic coherence to realize the script on screen.

questions.sub_topic: First Indian Cinema Screening: Lumiere Brothers in Bombay (1896)
questions.question: On July 7, 1896, the Lumière brothers' Cinématographe screened the very first moving motion pictures in India at which historic venue in Bombay?
options: A) Coronation Cinema
B) Watson's Hotel
C) Majestic Theatre
D) Elphinstone Picture Palace
questions.explanation: The Lumière brothers introduced cinema to India on July 7, 1896 at Watson's Hotel in Bombay, screening six short films hailed by The Times of India as 'the marvel of the century'.

questions.sub_topic: Depth of Field: Shallow vs Deep Focus
questions.question: In cinematic photography, what visual aesthetic characterizes a 'Shallow Depth of Field'?
options: A) Every object from two inches in front of the lens to infinity is in razor-sharp focus
B) The image appears completely pitch black without any illumination whatsoever
C) Only a narrow plane of the image (such as the actor's face) is in sharp focus, while the foreground and background are softly blurred
D) The film projection frame rotates three hundred sixty degrees continuously
questions.explanation: A shallow depth of field isolates the subject against a blurry, out-of-focus background (bokeh), directing viewer attention and creating cinematic visual intimacy.

questions.sub_topic: Soviet Montage Cinema: Lev Kuleshov and Battleship Potemkin
questions.question: Which historic 1925 Soviet silent masterpiece, directed by Sergei Eisenstein, demonstrated the power of metric and rhythmic montage in the famous 'Odessa Steps' sequence?
options: A) The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari
B) Man with a Movie Camera
C) The Passion of Joan of Arc
D) Battleship Potemkin
questions.explanation: Sergei Eisenstein's 'Battleship Potemkin' (1925) immortalized montage theory; the Odessa Steps massacre cuts between marching soldiers, fleeing citizens, and a careening baby carriage.

questions.sub_topic: Parallel Cinema Movement Pioneers: Shyam Benegal's Ankur (1974)
questions.question: Shyam Benegal's debut feature 'Ankur' (The Seedling, 1974), featuring Shabana Azmi, is celebrated in Indian cinema history for inaugurating the Middle Cinema/New Indian Cinema through its raw critique of:
options: A) Feudal oppression, caste hierarchies, rural economic exploitation, and patriarchal sexual domination in rural Andhra Pradesh
B) Interstellar spacecraft exploration missions across distant extraterrestrial solar systems
C) High-society ballroom waltz dance competitions in 19th-century colonial British mansions
D) Slapstick silent comedic routines featuring circus clowns and trained performing elephants
questions.explanation: Benegal's 'Ankur' broke Bollywood formulaic escapism, launching realistic Middle Cinema with uncompromising depictions of rural feudal exploitation, caste violence, and gender subjugation.

questions.sub_topic: Bazin's Deep Focus Aesthetics: Orson Welles' Citizen Kane (1941)
questions.question: Why did realist film theorist André Bazin revere Gregg Toland and Orson Welles' use of 'Deep Focus' cinematography in 'Citizen Kane' (1941)?
options: A) It allowed Orson Welles to act in the movie without wearing any physical actor costumes

B) It maintained all spatial planes (foreground, middleground, background) in sharp focus simultaneously, preserving spatial-temporal unity and allowing viewers freedom of visual choice rather than forcing montage manipulation
C) It was the first motion picture recorded entirely without using any glass camera lenses
D) It eliminated all dialogic speech and replaced it with classical Italian grand opera singing
questions.explanation: Bazin argued deep focus respects reality: by keeping all planes in focus in long takes, Welles preserved spatial continuity and granted spectators cognitive freedom to explore the composition.

questions.question: A word or phrase preceded by the pound symbol (#) used across social media platforms to categorize topics and track trending discussions is a:
options: A) Hyperlink
B) Firewall
C) Hashtag
D) Bandwidth
questions.explanation: A hashtag (#) categorizes content, aggregating related posts across a platform and facilitating topic discoverability.

questions.question: The repeated use of digital electronic communication (social media, text messages, or gaming channels) to intimidate, harass, threaten, or humiliate an individual is called:
options: A) Crowdfunding
B) Podcasting
C) Blogging
D) Cyberbullying
questions.explanation: Cyberbullying is targeted digital harassment, intimidation, or embarrassment carried out through electronic communications.

questions.question: How does Eli Pariser's concept of the 'Filter Bubble' limit an internet user's intellectual and political perspective?
options: A) Search engines and social media algorithms cater only to past behavioral clicks, showing users agreeable content while isolating them from opposing or challenging viewpoints
B) It physically filters out dust particles from computer keyboard ventilation holes
C) It forces users to look at computer monitors through spherical glass bubbles
D) It prevents users from connecting to the internet during rainy monsoon seasons
questions.explanation: Filter bubbles trap users in personalized information universes: predictive algorithms reinforce past biases by feeding familiar content while filtering out contradictory viewpoints.

questions.sub_topic: Social Media Influencer Sponsorships and Endorsements
questions.question: In digital influencer marketing, what ethical responsibility is legally mandated when an influencer receives payment or free luxury products to review a brand on their social channels?
options: A) They must keep the financial payment secret and claim they bought the product with their own money
B) They must clearly, conspicuously disclose the commercial sponsorship (e.g., using #Ad, #Sponsored, or #PaidPartnership) upfront to their followers
C) They must legally change their surname to the brand name of the sponsoring corporation
D) They must delete their social media user account immediately after publishing the review
questions.explanation: Global consumer protection bodies and ASCI guidelines mandate clear, transparent disclosures on all sponsored influencer content to prevent misleading consumer fraud.

questions.sub_topic: Surveillance Capitalism: Zuboff's Behavioral Futures Markets
questions.question: In Shoshana Zuboff's theory of Surveillance Capitalism, what are 'Behavioral Futures Markets'?
options: A) Agricultural commodity futures exchanges where farmers trade wheat and cotton harvest contracts
B) Stock exchanges where employees trade company shares based on physical employee attendance
C) Markets where algorithmic prediction products manufactured from harvested human behavioral data are bought and sold by commercial businesses to anticipate and modify consumer actions
D) Scientific laboratory facilities where researchers study the future genetic evolution of human behavior
questions.explanation: Zuboff defines behavioral futures markets as the economic trade where tech giants sell behavioral predictions (clicks, purchases, emotions) to advertisers seeking to influence future actions.

questions.question: According to the Claire Wardle and Hossein Derakhshan taxonomy of 'Information Disorder', what is the defining characteristic that separates 'Disinformation' from 'Misinformation'?
options: A) Disinformation is published only in hardcover books, while misinformation is spoken on FM radio
B) Disinformation is created exclusively by children, while misinformation is created by software engineers
C) Disinformation contains only true verified facts, while misinformation contains fictional poetry

D) Disinformation is false information deliberately created and weaponized with malicious intent to deceive and harm, whereas Misinformation is false information shared mistakenly without intent to cause harm
questions.explanation: The distinguishing factor is intent: Misinformation is false info shared innocently without harmful intent; Disinformation is intentionally crafted and circulated to mislead and harm.

questions.question: The asynchronous digital messaging technology that allows computer users to exchange written messages and computer files over the internet using standardized protocols is:
options: A) E-mail (Electronic Mail)
B) Teletext
C) Paging
D) Facsimile (Fax)
questions.explanation: Electronic mail (email) is a foundational internet protocol enabling rapid, asynchronous digital text and file transmission across distributed networks.

questions.question: In computer networking and internet communications, what does 'Bandwidth' refer to?
options: A) The physical width of a computer monitor frame measured in inches
B) The maximum data transfer capacity or rate of a network connection, measuring how much digital data can travel across a channel in a given time (e.g., Mbps)
C) The musical frequency of an electric guitar played in a broadcast studio
D) The number of journalists employed by a regional print newspaper
questions.explanation: Bandwidth measures the maximum volume of digital data (bits per second) that can travel across an internet network connection in a given time interval.

questions.question: A digital blog where the primary medium of expression and storytelling is video footage rather than written text is commonly called a:
options: A) Podcast
B) Press Release
C) Vlog (Video Blog)
D) Masthead
questions.explanation: A vlog (video blog) is a personal or topical blog presented primarily through video clips, widely popular on platforms like YouTube.

questions.question: In digital news website analytics and online advertising, what does 'Click-Through Rate' (CTR) measure?
options: A) The physical mechanical sound made by computer mice when clicked in office cubicles
B) The total number of computers connected to the World Wide Web in a single calendar year
C) The speed at which a computer monitor refreshes electrical video frames per second
D) The percentage of users who click on a specific headline, hyperlink, or advertisement out of the total number of users who viewed the page (Impressions)
questions.explanation: CTR (clicks divided by impressions multiplied by 100) measures engagement efficiency, showing what proportion of users exposed to a link or ad clicked on it.

questions.question: In Henry Jenkins' theory of 'Transmedia Storytelling', how is an expansive narrative universe (such as Marvel or Star Wars) constructed across platforms?
options: A) Narrative elements are dispersed across films, television shows, comic books, and video games, with each medium making a distinct, valuable contribution to the overall world
B) The exact same feature film is played on repeat across forty different movie channels simultaneously
C) All movie scripts are translated exclusively into ancient Latin and Sanskrit languages
D) The story is printed exclusively on cardboard cereal boxes distributed to school cafeterias
questions.explanation: Jenkins defines transmedia storytelling as a narrative dispersed across multiple media platforms, where each medium contributes unique storyworld content rather than mere redundant adaptation.

questions.topic: New Media: Cyber Ethics and Intellectual Property
questions.sub_topic: Fair Use Doctrine in Digital Content Creation
questions.question: Under intellectual property law, which four statutory factors determine whether a content creator's use of copyrighted material qualifies as legal 'Fair Use' (or Fair Dealing)?
options: A) The author's birth country; the computer brand used; the font size; and the internet connection speed
B) The number of followers; the time of day; the price of the camera; and the screen resolution
C) Whether the work was created in summer or winter; the language used; the paper weight; and the editor's age
D) Purpose/character of use (transformative/nonprofit); Nature of copyrighted work; Amount/substantiality used; and Effect upon the work's potential market value
questions.explanation: Fair use evaluates: 1) Purpose of use (transformative, criticism, education); 2) Nature of original work; 3) Amount taken relative to the whole; 4) Impact on the original market value.
